_description: Maps country + time period → available record types. MVP: US only (1790-1950).

records.notes: Federal census every 10 years. 1890 census largely destroyed by fire. State censuses also exist for some states.
Vital registration varies by state. Most states began mandatory registration between 1880-1920. Earlier records may exist in church or county records.
Similar to birth records — state-level registration began 1880-1920. Death certificates often include parents' names and birthplaces.
County-level marriage licenses and certificates. Some states have statewide indexes. Church records may predate civil records.

Revolutionary War (1775-1783), War of 1812, Mexican-American War (1846-1848), Civil War (1861-1865), Spanish-American War (1898), WWI (1917-1918), WWII (1941-1945). Service records, pension files, draft registrations.
Passenger arrival lists (ship manifests) from 1820. Castle Garden (1855-1890), Ellis Island (1892-1954). Earlier arrivals may appear in colonial records.
Filed in any federal, state, or local court. Post-1906 records are standardized and more detailed (include birthplace, arrival info). Pre-1906 records vary greatly.
County recorder deeds, federal land patents (General Land Office). Homestead Act records from 1862. Land records can establish residence and family connections.
Wills, estate inventories, guardianship records filed at county level. Often name family members and reveal economic status.
Obituaries, marriage announcements, legal notices, local news. Coverage increases dramatically after 1850. Digitized collections growing rapidly.
Baptism, marriage, burial records. May predate civil vital records. Availability depends on denomination and congregation survival. Catholic diocesan archives often centralized.
Annual directories listing residents, occupations, and addresses. Excellent for tracking urban ancestors between census years. Coverage best for cities and larger towns.
Headstone inscriptions and sexton records. FindAGrave and BillionGraves have digitized millions of markers. May include birth/death dates, family relationships.
Property tax rolls, personal property tax, federal direct tax (1798, 1813-1816). Useful for tracking residence and economic status between census years.
School censuses, enrollment records, yearbooks. Availability varies by district. Some states conducted school censuses that list all children in a household.
